analysis.one_liner: Strips major tax breaks from large investors that own 50 or more single-family rental homes.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on October 4, 2024 and died there when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal tax rules so that a company owning 50 or more single-family homes as rentals can no longer deduct the mortgage interest on those homes or take depreciation write-downs on them. Those two deductions are major tax advantages for landlords, so removing them makes it more expensive to hold large numbers of family homes as rentals. The bill includes an escape valve: when a covered landlord sells a home, those deductions are allowed again — but only if the buyer is an individual buying the home to live in, or a qualified nonprofit such as a community land trust or land bank. That design is meant to push big investors toward selling houses to families instead of to other investors. Newly built homes and low-income housing tax credit properties are exempt, so the bill does not penalize construction.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people trying to buy a home, and renters in neighborhoods where large investors have bought up houses. If the bill passed, big corporate landlords would face higher after-tax costs on 50 or more single-family rentals, giving them a reason to sell some homes — and the tax rules only let them keep the deductions if they sell to someone buying it to live in or to an affordable-housing nonprofit. That would put more houses on the market for would-be homeowners and for community land trusts. Small landlords with fewer than 50 properties are untouched, and newly built homes are exempt, so construction would not be discouraged.

how_it_helps.text: By denying interest and depreciation deductions, the bill raises the after-tax cost of owning 50 or more single-family rentals, which is designed to make corporate ownership of family homes less profitable and push some properties toward sale.

When a covered landlord sells, the deductions are only allowed if the buyer is an individual buying a home to live in or a qualified nonprofit such as a community land trust, land bank, or affordable-housing group — steering the housing stock toward owner-occupants and permanently affordable housing rather than another investor.
The tax penalty applies to the whole controlled group: related companies are counted as one owner, so an operator cannot avoid the threshold by spreading houses across affiliates.
Newly built homes and low-income housing tax credit properties are exempt, so the bill targets the buying up of existing homes, not the construction of new ones.

analysis.who_pays: Large investors — corporations, private equity, and similar owners holding 50 or more single-family rental homes — would lose the mortgage-interest and depreciation deductions on those properties, raising the cost of holding them. They could recover those deductions only by selling to an owner-occupant buyer or a qualified affordable-housing nonprofit. In the short run, some of the higher cost could be passed to tenants as rent, and the effect on home prices and availability would depend on how investors respond.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporate owners of many rental homes

drawbacks.text: Removing deductions raises large landlords' cost of doing business, and some of that cost could be passed to tenants as higher rents before any homes come up for sale.
The 50-property threshold means the change reaches only large operators; a mid-size landlord with 49 houses keeps all deductions, and the line between 49 and 50 is arbitrary.

Sophisticated investors may be able to restructure or split holdings to stay under the threshold; the bill only authorizes regulations to prevent avoidance, which would take time to write and could be contested.

The bill does nothing about supply directly; it relies entirely on tax pressure to change investor behavior, and any homes that come up for sale would still compete with other buyers in tight markets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real: denying interest and depreciation deductions to owners of 50+ single-family rentals raises the cost of holding large numbers of family homes as rentals, which should push some of them onto the market for buyers and could slow the conversion of neighborhoods into corporate rental portfolios. The costs and caveats are genuine: rents would not fall immediately, landlords' higher costs could show up as rent increases in the short run, and large operators have easy workarounds (leasing rather than owning homes, spreading holdings across unaffiliated entities) that the bill only addresses through regulations the Treasury Secretary would have to write. Whether the tax change is enough to change investor behavior, or whether the 50-property threshold is too high to matter for many mid-size operators, no committee ever examined, because the bill never received a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in October 2024, sent to the tax-writing committee, and the Congress ended before anyone acted on it.

narrative.text: The House introduced the bill on October 4, 2024, less than three months before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill's only action beyond introduction was a referral to the House Committee on Ways and Means on October 4, 2024; the record shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action.
Because the bill died at the end of the 118th Congress, it would have to be reintroduced from scratch in the next Congress to move again.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporate owners of single-family rental homes are better off: they keep the mortgage-interest and depreciation deductions the bill would have taken away, and face no new pressure to sell homes to buyers or nonprofits. Ordinary homebuyers gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Emilia Sykes
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House on October 4, 2024.

for.name: Rep. Dwight Evans and Rep. Nydia Velázquez
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Ways and Means Committee (Chair Jason Smith)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on October 4, 2024 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat with two Democratic cosponsors and died in committee without any votes, so no Republicans ever went on record on it; the Ways and Means committee that controlled its fate had a Republican majority and chair.

industries.industry: Large corporate single-family rental landlords (institutional investors with 50+ homes)
industries.note: The bill strips away two of their biggest tax benefits — deducting mortgage interest and depreciation — making it more expensive to hold large portfolios of family homes, and gives them a tax break only if they sell to a homebuyer or a nonprofit. This directly targets the business model of buying up existing houses to rent out.

industries.industry: Affordable housing nonprofits, community land trusts, land banks, and resident-owned cooperatives
industries.note: When a covered landlord sells, the tax break applies only if the buyer is a homebuyer or one of these organizations, so the bill creates an incentive to route sales of previously investor-owned homes to nonprofits that keep them affordable.

industries.industry: Small and mid-size landlords (fewer than 50 properties)
industries.note: They are untouched by the deduction ban, and if large operators sell off homes, smaller landlords compete for the homes alongside families. A landlord near the threshold could face pressure not to expand, but most are unaffected.

New construction is exempt from the deduction ban, so building homes to sell or rent keeps full tax treatment; the bill only penalizes acquiring existing homes. Homebuilders are largely left out of the fight.
